lesson.title: Concave Down: When the Graph Spills Over
lesson.summary: A function is concave down on exactly the intervals where f'' is negative, meaning its slope is continually decreasing there, giving the graph the shape of a dome rather than a bowl.
lesson.body:
An interval where f''(x) is less than 0 for every x in it is called concave down. On such an interval f' is a decreasing function, so tangent lines drawn to the graph sit above the curve rather than below it, touching at one point and then the curve falls away underneath as x moves in either direction. That is the shape of a dome, or a hill, water would slide off it rather than pool in it.

For f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5, the concave down interval was found earlier to be (negative infinity, 1), using f''(x) = 6(x - 1). Checking x = -3 confirms it: f''(-3) = 6(-3 - 1) = 6(-4) = -24, negative, agreeing with the earlier test at x = 0. Some functions are concave down across their whole domain. For f(x) = -x^2, f''(x) = -2, a negative constant, so the downward parabola is concave down everywhere. For f(x) = ln(x), defined for x greater than 0, f'(x) = 1/x and f''(x) = -1/x^2, which is negative for every x in the domain, so the natural logarithm curve is concave down across its entire graph, its growth continually slowing even though it never stops increasing.

Tangent lines on a concave down interval always sit above the actual curve, giving an overestimate of the function's true values nearby. This is also why a critical point sitting inside a concave down region, where f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) is less than 0, must be a local maximum: the graph rises up to meet the tangent line at c, but the dome shape means it can only fall away on both sides after that, exactly what the Second Derivative Test predicts.
